passage: Ganga, you asked why your father tells such jokes when he is sad, so sit and listen. I am Minakshi, your Dadi. When your father Ravi was fourteen, his team lost the kabaddi final, and he came home with red eyes. His father said, "Boys don't cry. Wipe your face." Ravi did. By evening he was doing the referee's voice for everyone, and by night he snapped at his sister for touching his shoes. I saw that the jokes were a lid. That night I sat beside him on the stairs and said nothing for a long time. Then I said, "I cried for days when my own grandmother died. It's allowed." Ravi's shoulders dropped and he cried against my arm. His father, in the doorway, said nothing that night. The next morning he brought Ravi his tea himself.

qa.q: What happened at the kabaddi final?
qa.a: Ravi's team lost the kabaddi final, and he came home with red eyes.

qa.q: How did Ravi feel after being told "Boys don't cry", and how could Minakshi tell?
qa.a: Ravi felt sad and probably ashamed of it. He hid it behind jokes and then snapped at his sister, which Minakshi saw as a lid.

qa.q: What choice did Minakshi make that night that helped Ravi?
qa.a: She sat beside him quietly for a long time instead of scolding, then told him she had cried for days too and that it was allowed.

qa.q: How might Ravi's father have felt watching from the doorway?
qa.a: Probably unsettled and thoughtful, since he said nothing and the next morning he brought Ravi tea himself.

grounding: A boy is told to be strong and stop crying, hides sadness behind jokes and anger, and is helped by someone who lets him be sad.

passage: The house was full of relatives for the thirteenth-day rites, and there was no quiet corner anywhere. Tarun, fifteen, had not cried once since his grandfather died. "You're the eldest grandson now, be strong, no tears," an uncle told him. Tarun laughed too loudly and did impressions of the priest for the cousins. When his older cousin Jomon asked, "You okay?" Tarun snapped, "Why wouldn't I be? Leave it." Jomon didn't argue. Later, on the crowded terrace stairs, Jomon sat down two steps below him with two cups of tea. "I cried in the bathroom for an hour when my nana died," Jomon said. "No one heard." Tarun stared at the cup. Then his shoulders shook, and Jomon kept sitting there.

qa.q: Who told Tarun to be strong and shed no tears?
qa.a: An uncle told him to be strong, with no tears.

qa.q: Why did Tarun snap at Jomon, and what was Tarun feeling underneath?
qa.a: Tarun snapped because the question came too close to the grief he was hiding. Underneath he felt sad and overwhelmed.

qa.q: What choice did Jomon make on the stairs that changed the moment?
qa.a: Jomon sat down quietly with tea and shared crying in the bathroom too, without pushing, so Tarun could let go.

qa.q: How might Jomon see Tarun's jokes and anger?
qa.a: Jomon may see them as a way of covering grief, so Jomon does not argue but waits for a quieter moment.

grounding: A boy is told to be strong and stop crying, hides sadness behind jokes and anger, and is helped by someone who shares their own tears.

passage:
The calf died on a Tuesday morning, and Suraj, fourteen, found her in the shed. He had fed her by hand since she was born.
He sat in the straw and cried until his chest hurt. His uncle came to the door. "Arre, a boy crying over a calf? Be strong. Get up."
Suraj wiped his face fast and laughed too loudly. "Just dust in my eyes, Chacha." At school he joked about it all day.
That evening his elder sister Gargi found him behind the well, kicking stones. She sat down next to him. "You loved her. It's okay to be sad."
Suraj stopped kicking. Then he cried again, and Gargi let him. Later, she told their mother what Chacha had said, and their mother told Chacha firmly, "Let the boy grieve."

qa.q: Who found the calf in the shed?
qa.a: Suraj, fourteen, found her in the shed.

qa.q: Why did Suraj laugh too loudly and joke all day?
qa.a: Suraj was hiding his grief and shame after his uncle told him to be strong, covering sadness with jokes.

qa.q: How did Gargi and their mother help Suraj?
qa.a: Gargi sat with him and said it was okay to be sad, and their mother told Chacha firmly to let him grieve, protecting his honesty about his feelings.

qa.q: How might Chacha's words affect Suraj in the future?
qa.a: If nobody had stepped in, Suraj might keep learning that boys must hide sadness behind jokes or anger.

grounding: A boy is told to be strong and stop crying, hides grief behind jokes and anger, and family members protect his right to feel sad.

passage:
After Lars missed the penalty in the under-16 final in Gothenburg, he sat on the bench with his hands over his face. His shoulders were shaking.
"Stop crying, Lars," one of the fathers called from the stands. "Be a man about it."
Lars dropped his hands and grinned. "Guess I'll be a goalkeeper," he joked. His teammate Kwame didn't laugh. For the next week Lars laughed at everything and snapped at anyone who mentioned the match.
On Friday, the coach asked Lars and Kwame to stay behind. "I cried after I lost my first final," the coach said. "It meant I cared. Nobody gets to take that from you."
Lars stared at his boots for a long time. Then he said, "It felt like I let everyone down."
Kwame nudged him. "You didn't. You were brave enough to take it."

qa.q: Where was the under-16 final?
qa.a: The under-16 final was in Gothenburg.

qa.q: Why did Lars joke and snap at people all week?
qa.a: He was hiding his sadness and shame after being told to be a man, so he covered it with jokes and irritation.

qa.q: What did the coach do that helped Lars?
qa.a: The coach shared a personal story and said crying meant caring, which made it safe for Lars to say he felt he let everyone down.

qa.q: How might Kwame see Lars's jokes?
qa.a: Kwame doesn't laugh, so he probably sees the jokes as a cover for how hurt Lars really is, and he wants to reassure him.

grounding: Outside India, a boy is told to stop crying, hides sadness behind jokes and anger, and an adult protects his emotional honesty.

passage:
In the boys' hostel at the residential school, the rule was simple: nobody cried where anyone could see. Abhinav, fifteen, learned it in his first week, when a senior mocked a boy who missed home.
So when his grandfather died in March, Abhinav punched the washroom door instead. He picked a fight at football. He told jokes at dinner until even his friends went quiet.
The warden, Chaitanya Sir, called him to the office the next evening. He didn't ask about the fight first. He said, "I heard about your grandfather. I'm sorry."
Abhinav's jaw worked. "I'm fine, sir."
"You don't have to be fine here," Chaitanya Sir said quietly, and shut the door.
Abhinav cried for twenty minutes. Chaitanya Sir waited, then called his mother so they could talk, and arranged for him to see the school counsellor the next morning.

qa.q: Who called Abhinav to the office?
qa.a: The warden, Chaitanya Sir, called him to the office.

qa.q: What does Abhinav punching the washroom door suggest he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt deep grief and anger, but couldn't show sadness openly because of the hostel's rule.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya Sir do well?
qa.a: He began with the grandfather's death rather than the fight, said Abhinav didn't have to be fine, waited while he cried, then called his mother and arranged a counsellor visit.

qa.q: How might Abhinav's friends feel when he tells jokes until they go quiet?
qa.a: They may feel uneasy and worried, sensing that the jokes are covering something painful.

grounding: In a hostel, a boy who has learned not to cry hides grief behind anger and jokes, and an adult protects his emotional honesty.

passage:
Dear Sumit bhaiya,
I wanted to write this because I can't say it on the phone. When Dadaji died last month, I cried at the cremation, in front of everyone. Papa put his hand on my shoulder and said, "Be strong. Boys don't cry." One of the uncles laughed and said, "Look at him, like a girl." So I stopped. Since then I make jokes all the time. At school I got into a fight over nothing. Mummy says I've become "so rude". I don't know how to explain that it's all inside and has nowhere to go.
Then I remembered: at Dadaji's house, the night after, I saw you crying on the terrace. You didn't hide. You just said, "I miss him." That's the only time I felt normal.
Can I call you when it gets bad? I don't want to joke about everything anymore.
Darshan

qa.q: What did Papa say at the cremation?
qa.a: "Be strong. Boys don't cry."

qa.q: How has Darshan been feeling since the cremation?
qa.a: Darshan has been sad and angry inside, hiding grief behind jokes and even fighting at school.

qa.q: How can Sumit bhaiya support Darshan?
qa.a: He can say yes to calls, listen without mocking, and show again that missing someone and crying are normal.

qa.q: How might Papa see his words at the cremation?
qa.a: Papa probably thought he was helping Darshan be brave, without realising it taught him to hide his sadness.

grounding: It illustrates a boy told not to cry who hides sadness behind jokes and anger, and an older cousin whose honesty protects his feelings.
